title: Section XII. Of the academical or sceptical Philosophy
author: David Hume
summary: Hume rejects excessive Pyrrhonian scepticism as unliveable, and recommends a mitigated scepticism that confines enquiry to common life and experience. Books that contain neither abstract reasoning about quantity nor experimental reasoning about fact should be committed to the flames.

notes.note: The method of Descartes's *Meditations* (1641): doubt everything that can be doubted until something certain is found.

notes.on: or the excessive principles of scepticism
notes.note: *Pyrrhonism*: the radical scepticism of Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360–c. 270 BC), known chiefly through the writings of Sextus Empiricus.
Hume's note names George Berkeley (1685–1753), whose argument against abstract ideas opens his *Principles of Human Knowledge* (1710).
*Natural philosophy*: physics and the natural sciences; *physic*: medicine.
*Divinity*: theology. *School metaphysics*: the scholastic philosophy of the medieval and early modern universities.

notes.on: Commit it then to the flames
notes.note: The logical positivists of the twentieth century took this passage as a forerunner of their own rejection of metaphysics.
